319.text: The man who brought the Kotze name to South Africa. Born in Königstein in Saxony, Jan was a merchant who arrived at the Cape on the ship Pampas on 13 May 1691, coming as a paying passenger rather than as a Company servant. He married three times: first in Germany to Catharina Henneka, then at the Cape to Hillegonda Boon, and in 1704 to Hendrina van Hoeting. Cape records also show him buying and selling enslaved people, a hard but real part of life at the early Cape. Through his son Dirk, he is the ancestor of the Kotzés in this tree.

305.text: Jan Kotze's Cape-born son by Hillegonda Boon, remembered in family genealogies as 'Rooi Dirk' (Red Dirk). He farmed in the Drakenstein valley near today's Paarl and carried the Kotze line into its first South African generations.

322.text: Mom's tree links Jan Kotze, who sailed to the Cape, to the Saxon noble family von Kotze. Their seat was the estate of Groß Germersleben near Magdeburg, and the state archives of Saxony-Anhalt still hold centuries of von Kotze papers: debts, leases and inheritance files running from the 1500s into the 1800s.

330.text: A lord of the von Kotze estate at Germersleben in Saxony. Regional archives record the family's dealings over the estate in his lifetime, including a claim by the cathedral chapter of Magdeburg against the von Kotze heirs that was first filed in 1571 and dragged on for nearly a century.

227.text: A French Huguenot refugee from Normandy, who came to the Cape with his brother Estienne after Protestants were driven out of France. In February 1699 he was granted a farm in the Wagenmakers Valley near today's Wellington, which he named Versailles. He married Suzanne Taillefert, a widow from another refugee family, and their surname gradually became Cronjé. A newspaper in 1900 traced the famous Boer general Piet Cronjé back to him.

226.text: Suzanne came from a Huguenot family of Château-Thierry in Champagne; her father Isaac was a vine-grower and hatmaker. The family sailed on the Oosterland, the first ship of the great Huguenot emigration, which reached Table Bay on 26 April 1688. At the Cape she was first married to another refugee, Jean Gardé, and as his widow she married Pierre Cronier, so she is a mother of the Cronjé family.

234.text: Jean Roy (Rey in Provençal) was a winegrower from Lourmarin in Provence, of Vaudois Protestant stock. Three years after France outlawed Protestantism he fled, reaching the Cape on 4 August 1688. He was given land at the foot of the Drakenstein mountains near Franschhoek and named the farm L'Ormarins after his home village, a name the wine estate still carries today. In 1712 he married Marie-Catherine le Febre.

233.text: One of the very first children of French descent born at the Cape: her baptism in 1686 was the first recorded at Stellenbosch. She outlived three husbands, the Huguenots Gabriel le Roux and Jean Roi and later Frans Haarhoff, and moved with her family to the far frontier at Swellendam. She died at the mouth of the Gouritz River in 1782, aged about 96, having lived through almost a century of the colony's history.

612.text: Abraham and his brothers Jacques and Pierre were Huguenot refugees from Normandy, living in exile at Zierikzee in Zeeland. The local Walloon church gave them a last handout 'for the three departing Viviers' before they sailed for the Cape on 24 April 1688. Abraham married sixteen-year-old Jacquemine des Prez when he was 41 and farmed at Drakenstein. All three brothers died in the smallpox epidemic of 1713.

617.text: Born Jacquemine des Prez, from a Huguenot family of French Flanders. She married Abraham Vivier at sixteen and had eight children with him. After Abraham died in the smallpox epidemic of 1713 she was widowed with a baby on the way; her daughter Anna was baptised at Drakenstein in January 1714, and Jacquemine died later that year. Her sister Marie-Jeanne and brother-in-law Jacques Therond raised the five Vivier girls.

1237.text: The founding father of the van Zyl family in South Africa. Born in Delft, the son of a tinsmith, he married Christina van Loveren in Amsterdam in 1694 and went to the Cape, first as a gardener for the Dutch East India Company and then as a free farmer at Vrede en Lust near Paarl. In 1705–06 he joined Adam Tas and Henning Hüsing in drawing up the famous petition against Governor Willem Adriaan van der Stel's corruption. The burghers won: the Company recalled the governor in 1707.

2236.text: Charlemagne, the most famous ruler of the early Middle Ages. King of the Franks from 768 and of the Lombards from 774, he was crowned Emperor by Pope Leo III in Rome on Christmas Day 800. He united much of western Europe under one rule and sponsored a revival of learning, and he is often called the 'Father of Europe'.

2241.text: Charlemagne's beloved queen, married to him as a young girl around 771. She travelled with him on campaign and bore him nine children, including the future emperor Louis the Pious, before dying in 783 when she was only about 25.

2233.text: Louis the Pious, Charlemagne's son and heir, emperor from 814 to 840. Quarrels among his sons after his death led to the Treaty of Verdun in 843, which split the empire into three. The western and eastern parts grew into France and Germany.

2251.text: Bertrada of Laon, Pepin's queen and Charlemagne's mother, remembered in medieval legend as 'Bertha Broadfoot' (Berthe au grand pied). She was a respected adviser to her son in his early reign.

2253.text: Charles Martel, 'the Hammer', grandfather of Charlemagne. As mayor of the palace he was the real power in the Frankish kingdom, and in 732 he defeated an invading Umayyad army near Tours and Poitiers, one of the most famous battles of the age.

2398.text: Alfred, King of Wessex from 871 to 899, and the only English king called 'the Great'. He held out against the Viking Great Heathen Army, won a decisive victory at Edington in 878, built fortified towns and a navy, and championed learning in English. He is also the hero of the old tale of the burnt cakes.

2451.text: Hengist and his brother Horsa are the legendary leaders said to have brought the first Saxons to Britain in the 5th century and founded the kingdom of Kent. Their story comes from Bede and later chroniclers, and historians treat it as part history, part legend.

2140.text: Dirk II, Count in West Frisia, the lands that grew into the County of Holland. He and his wife Hildegard gave the beautiful Egmond Gospels to Egmond Abbey, and the book still contains a picture of the couple presenting it.

2626.text: King Lucius, the legendary 'first Christian king of Britain'. The story appears in an early list of popes and was repeated by Bede. Modern historians think the story grew from a mix-up with a different king named Lucius.
